THE HERBERT L. BRIDGMAN
DIAMOND MEMORIAL FUND
EVERY
Psi U. a life subscriber of The Diamond!"
With this ambitious slogan, a determined drive has been launched
by the Board of Editors to complete the raising of a $100,000
permanent endowment fund for the publication of the fraternity's official
journal.
Every alumnus brother whose name is not already on the roll of life
subscribers will be solicited during the coming months and urged to fall in
line.
The medium of solicitation will be a handsome four page folder setting
forth the history of the Herbert L. Bridgman Diamond Memorial Fund and
the purpose of the present campaign. Upon the title page of the folder, the
crest of the fraternity is finely engraved; the whole page, bordered with
gold, is an admirable example of the engraver's art; it is reproduced else
where in this issue.
This splendid piece of direct-mail publicity and other important aux
iliaries of the campaign have been made possible by a gift of $1000 by
Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, retiring president of the Executive Council.
This material will be mailed out to approximately 14,000 alumni
brothers. Through the sale of life subscriptions at $10 each since the estab
lishment of the Memorial Fund five years ago, a total of $25,000 has
been realized. In view of the fact that no determined canvass of alumni
brothers has been made, this sum represented a very satisfactory achieve
ment
But it is not enough to ensure the publication of The Diamond, in
perpetuity. Hence the present drive. The fund is administered as a trust
fund by the Executive Council. From it no salaries are paid except for
stenographic help. The editors contribute their services without remuner
ation.
The dedication of The Diamond Fund to the late Brother Bridgman
was inspired both by his long and able service as president of the fraternity,
and by his unfailing belief in the future of the publication itself. The folder
being mailed to non-subscribing brothers quotes a message from the pen
of Brother Bridgman published in The Diajwond of November, 1920, when
this now healthy publication awoke from a Rip Van Winkle slumber of 33
years of non-publication.

146 THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON
Wrote Brother Bridgman:
"Greeting
"The Diamond of Psi Upsilon inherits an honorable past, and faces
an inviting and useful future. Between official and individual trenches is
a wide and fruitful No Man's Land, which, cultivated with diligence and
intelligence, should yield power and prestige to the Fratemity. News�
general, chapter and personal, is always vital; history, tradition and remi
niscence instructive; discussion, if candid and sincere, stimulating and
prophetic; in short, there is no limit to service and usefulness provided loyalty
and independence are fearless and absolute. Unless The New Diamond lives
on merit, and on that alone, it were better it had never been born. The
mission of The New Diamond, as I see it, is to promote the welfare of the
whole Fraternity, not of any man or group in it; cherish and vitalize its
memories, elevate and advance its ideals, to translate them into the true
scholar, the loyal friend and the real gentleman."
Heretofore, life subscriptions have been sold for $10, and no larger or
smaller funds were accepted. During the present campaign, any offered
contribution will be accepted and used to swell the endowment fund. While
brothers who are
already life subscribers will not again be solicited, their
voluntary contributions will be welcome.

Thus on Monday, February 14th last, the Executive Council gathered

retiring from the council he wished to assure us of his readiness to perform
any task assigned where he could help in furthering any ideals or interests of

WILLIAM BUTTERWORTH ETA '89
BLAZES THE TRAIL
IN
THE van of that group of business leaders who are
guiding the Ameri
can nation into greener and more fertile fields of prosperity marches
Brother William Butterworth, Eta '89.
Brother Butterworth, as president of the Chamber of Commerce of the
United States, is directing the efforts of that important organization in
dredging out and deepening the channels of the American business stream.
Wasteful methods of distribution, cumbersome legislation that impedes
legitimate business, hazy and non-committal policies on the part of the
government on such important questions as that of water power develop
ment are among the sandbars which lie in the path of Brother Butterworth's
ambitious steam-shovel.
The same energy that brought him to the important position which he
now holds and that promises to make his regime a fruitful one was mani
fested during his college days at Lehigh. There he played Varsity baseball
and football, sang in the Glee Club, participated in dramatics, and edited
the college publication.
In a recent interview in the New York Times, Brother Butterworth dis
cussed various weighty problems toward whose solution the Chamber is
working:
"The sustaining of national prosperity through the removal of obstacles
to the free interchange of goods throughout the United States, whether these
obstacles are set up by government or by business itself.
"The carrying on of business transactions with the minimum of waste
and lost motion.
"Elimination of business abuses and the bringing about of a fuller
realization of the responsibilities of business toward the public.
"Advancement of the public interest through adaptation of distribution
methods to changing conditions.
"The more efficient spending of public funds raised by State and local
taxation.
"Simplification of the complexity of governmental machinery.
"Removal of the handicaps imposed on American concerns doing busi
ness in States other than those in which they are
incorporated.
"The assurance of protection to business as
existing in laws giving
Federal courts jurisdiction in suits between citizens of different States.

THE NEW PSI UPSILON CATALOGUE
FOR
a
long time there has been talk of a new catalogue inasmuch as a
very large percentage of the addresses given in the 1917 catalogue
are now incorrect. Then, too, we have initiated twelve delegations
into each of our chapters since 1917 and withal the development of alumni
activities has been seriously handicapped.
We realize that the most important asset of Psi Upsilon is its splendid
alumni roll and it is necessary to keep an accurate list of all data pertaining
to it. Thus the Executive Council has succeeded in getting Brother R.
Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15 to undertake this big task. It was felt that
inasmuch as he maintains the Diamond files in Chicago, he could best handle
this important work there, provided he was enabled to hire the necessary
clerical assistance. The Executive Council has appropriated $1200.00 to
cover this preliminary work and now the work is in actual progress. The
time for the appearance of this new catalogue will depend entirely upon the
promptness and thoroughness with which the alumni and undergraduate
masters of the rolls of the several chapters, respond to the requests of Brother
Corcoran.
The new catalogue will contain the names, addresses and occupations of
all alumni and undergraduate members. These will be listed by chapters in
classes and then there will be an alphabetical and geographical listing as
well. There will doubtless be a brief historical sketch of the fraternity and
other vital data printed in the front of the book. From all this there may
be issued a complete catalogue similar to the 1917 edition, in time for the
centennial.
All alumni are requested to give prompt attention to all mailings asking
for information and verification of addresses. In this way it is possible the
new catalogue may be ready by next fall.

HIS HONOUR JUDGE JOHN MULCAHY
NU '01
In this issue we reproduce a
photograph of His Honour Judge Mulcahy,
one of the founders and most highly esteemed brothers of The Nu, who was
recently appointed County Court Judge for the County of Renfrew, in the
Province of Ontario. In his undergraduate days, his genial personality
was one of the centres of the patience, enthusiasm and high ideals which
bound the members of the local organization to the policy which resulted
in the extension of Psi U to Toronto. He was actively interested in all Uni
versity affairs and graduated with honours in Arts in 1901. In 1904 he
obtained his honour diploma in law, and since that time has been a leading
member of the legal profession at Orillia. He is to be congratulated on the
success and the well earned reputation for integrity, industry and sound
judgment which have resulted in his selection by the Dominion Government
to preside over the Judicial affairs of this important county during the rest
of his life.
The loyalty and affection with which he regards the fraternity is indi
cated in the fact that his son, Tom, who has entered upon his studies at
Toronto, is following in father's footsteps, both fraternally and academically.
The Nu is proud of the past record of this distinguished graduate; it
is confident that he will adorn the position to which he has been elevated;
it looks forward to the time when it will have the opportunity of admitting
Tom's younger brothers and it hopes all his sisters may be captured by Psi
U's of their Dad's own type.
HOW TO STUDY
The Fraternity of Phi Gamma Delta has recently published an inter
esting book, entitled "A Manual on How to Study." The book is an
official publication of the Fratemity prepared, under the auspices of the
Permanent Committee on Scholarship, by Riverda Harding Jordan, Yale
'93. It constitutes real evidence of the serious interest the fraternities are
taking these days in the matter of scholarship.
The book calls for a series of weekly lessons to be held during the

freshman's first semester, with periodic reports to the chapter from the
faculty of every freshman's class work. Specific lessons, with specific
outside reading, are furnished for these meetings, with a written examina
tion at the end of the course.
The balance of the book consists of two long articles�
one entitled
"Conquering the Curriculum," written by Mr. Jordan, and the other
"Batting .300 in College," by Charles W. Hill, Minnesota '05, Wisconsin
'07. Mr. Jordan's article deals with such matters as the necessary mental
attitude, technique of study, adjusting the freshman to college, how to pre
pare for examinations, how to take notes, goals for advancement, and the
like.
Mr. Jordan's article contains some very interesting statistical material,
graphically brought home by the use of charts, showing the uses to which
college men put their time.
At first blush one
naturally wonders if good scholarship can be pro
duced by a text book, but this book certainly does contain a great deal of
valuable material on the subject of how to study, and a definite schedule of
regular instruction along that line is an important step in the right direction.
Phi Gamma Delta reports, too, that the principles and practices set forth in
the book have materially reduced freshman mortality.

FRANK A. KETCHAM, PHI '97
Elected President of the Graybar Electric Company
In December the Western Electric Company announced that it would
sell its associated company. The Graybar Electric Company, to the employees

The Graybar Electric is the largest electrical supply company in the

Brother Ketcham's election to the Presidency of this company is there
fore a mark of the real esteem in which his fellow employees hold him.
Mr. Ketcham started to work for the Chicago office of the company he
now heads in 1900. After serving his apprenticeship in the stock room, he
worked through the various clerical positions and in 1906 became chief
clerk. A year later he was advanced to the assistant managership and in 1911
became manager. In 1918, he advanced to the executive office in New York
as general manager and with the formation of the Graybar Electric Co. to
succeed the supply department of the Western Electric, Mr. Ketcham became
executive vice-president.

THE RHO OF PSI UPSILON
The installation of a new
chapter is a great event in the history of Psi
Upsilon; an event which, prior to last month, had occurred only eleven times
during more than half a century. After the establishment of the Mu in the
University of Minnesota five years ago, attention was directed to the inter
vening state of Wisconsin, and to its well-endowed and rapidly growing
University. By a fortunate turn of affairs the opportunity which Psi Upsilon
had rejected forty years before again presented itself.
THE UNIVERSITY OF WISCONSIN
This institution, which must be ranked among the first twelve of Ameri
can universities, opened its doors to students in 1849, the year following the
admission of Wisconsin as a State. In 1854, the first class, consisting of two
young men, was graduated from the academic department. Now the alumni
number 1,600, and there are more than 2,700 graduates. Since the year 1889
the progress of the institution has been very rapid. The number of students
has increased from 722 to 1,800. The University stands at the head of the

educational system of the State, its relations with the high schools and
academies is intimate, and it is not much troubled by opposition from
private colleges. The requirements for admission, and the character of
instruction, have always been high. For work in its graduate courses the
University has established for itself an enviable name.
One hundred and fifteen professors, assistant professors and instructors,
constitute the Faculty, at the head of which stands President Charles Kendall
Adams, LL.D. (Phi '61), one time Professor of History in the University
of Michigan, and later President of Cornell University, Another graduate
member of the Phi, the distinguished astronomer, James Craig Watson (Phi
'57), died in the service of this University for which he had reluctantly given
up his Alma Mater. Edward T. Owen (Beta '71) , is Professor of the French
Language and Literature; Amos A. Knowlton (Kappa '86), is Assistant
Professor of Rhetoric; and William S. Marshall, Ph.D. (Tau '89), is In
structor in Biology.
The libraries of the University contain 40,000 volumes, and are to be
housed, in connection with the unrivalled collection of the Wisconsin His
torical Society, in an extensive fireproof building for which the l^islation
of the State has appropriated $200,000. Among the buildings already erected
are Main Hall, South Hall, and North Hall, all of stone; Science Hall, a
structure of pressed brick, which cost $325,000; the Law Building, of brown
sandstone; Washburn Observatory; the Gymnasium and Armory, paid for
by a
legislative appropriation of $120,000; Library Hall, and the Chemical
Laboratory.
The endowment and income of the University are based upon and de
rived from federal land-grants, a tax upon mining companies, a permanent
tax of an eighth of a mill upon the assessed property in the State, and special
appropriations by the legislature.
The location of the University is one of great beauty. Professor Bryce
in "The American Commonwealth" speaks of the spacious grounds of the
University, which include "College HiU" and skirt for a long distance the
shores of Lake Mendota.
THE CITY OF MADISON
This town of 14,000 inhabitants, the capital of Wisconsin, and the seat
of the University, is situated on a prairie isthmus between Lakes Mendota
and Monona, with two other lakes lying near by. It was of Madison that
Longfellow wrote:

The city has many fine churches and private residences, and good
hotels. Its refined social atmosphere reminds one of Hartford and Provi

accessible to the Psi U. men.
EARLY PSI UPSILONISM IN WISCONSIN
Among the pioneers of the young Commonwealth were twenty or more
Psi Upsilons, graduates of Eastern colleges, who retained in Western wilds
their love for the Fratemity. Of these may be named the lamented Perry H.
Smith (Psi '46), one of the charter members of the Psi, and subsequently
a great railroad magnate, an active assistant in the foundation of the Omega,
and the father of two Psi U. sons; General Albert C. Ingham (Theta '47),
also an initiate of the Psi, through whose labors the revival of the Theta
was accomplished in 1865; Morris R. Barteau (Psi '45), who has been for
many years a manufacturer and merchant at Appleton, Wisconsin; and Jabez
Brooks (Psi '50), now Professor of Greek in the University of Minnesota.
On the evening of Thursday, January 23, 1851, these men and their
comrades met at Madison, and held what they called "The First Annual Con
vention of the Members of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity, resident in the State
of Wisconsin." Of their proceedings, duly printed in pamphlet form, a
copy is in the writer's hands, and contains the following resolutions:

What would have been the effect upon the social life of the University
had a chapter of Psi Upsilon been formed in Wisconsin before 1860, we

fraternity less

Psi Upsilon.
Though always faithful in the discharge of its fraternity duties, the

REMEMBER YOUR FRATERNITY
IN YOUR WILL
SURELY
there is no finer way to make a concrete showing of your
love for the loyal brotherly friendships brought into your life by your
election into Psi Upsilon.
Several of our
chapters have been the recipients of goodly sized bequests
within the last few years, and it is but fitting that it should ever be so. Like
wise the national fraternity funds might well be included. Some alumni
have not had this thought brought to their attention before and perhaps
many did not think of it as their own chapters were in excellent financial
condition with their homes free from indebtedness. It is not the purpose of
the fraternity to accumulate vast sums of money, but there are many pieces
of good work that could be done if the funds were available. Thus as an
example we could create a loan fund for deserving undergraduates after
their first year, or create scholarships and prizes for scholastic attainments.
